strengths: The paper identifies a relevant and underexplored problem for embodied AI: manipulating user-specific object instances such as “my cup” among same-category distractors, rather than only following generic object-category instructions.

VAP is simple, practical, and well matched to the problem: reference-image memory, open-vocabulary detection, DINOv2 matching, SAM2 segmentation/tracking, visual highlighting, and instruction rewriting provide a training-free adapter for frozen VLAs.

The evaluation is broader than many robotics submissions: two personalized simulation benchmarks, multiple robot embodiments, multi-view settings, and a real-world SO-101 tabletop setup with both selection and pick-and-place tasks.

Reported gains are large and consistent. For example, VAP substantially improves SR/CMR on Personalized-SIMPLER, improves all five Personalized-VLABench categories, and raises real-world average SR from 30.0% to 80.0% for pointing and from 18.8% to 56.2% for pick-and-place.

The paper includes useful baselines, including language hard prompts and a token-learning baseline, and the appendix gives a thoughtful analysis of why learned personalized tokens do not reliably translate into closed-loop control.

The limitations and error analysis are unusually concrete: the authors break down failures into single-view grounding errors, multi-view inconsistency, and correct-prompt-but-failed-control cases, which helps readers understand where the method actually fails.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is modest. The method is mainly a pipeline composition of existing open-vocabulary detection, DINO-style retrieval, SAM2 tracking, visual prompting, and string-based instruction rewriting. This is useful, but less original than the framing and evaluation might suggest.

The central claims are strongest only for a narrow setting: tabletop, short-horizon tasks, one personalized object at a time, known generic category extractable from “my X,” and a small number of visually similar distractors. The paper’s broader language about personalized robotic assistance is only partially supported.

The method depends heavily on strong external perception modules. When detection, matching, segmentation, or multi-view tracking fails, VAP fails; the paper reports this honestly, but it also means the contribution is less clearly a VLA personalization method than an upstream grounding-and-highlighting wrapper.

The evaluation lacks some important ablations and controls: oracle grounding/prompting to separate VLA limitations from perception limitations, component ablations for detection vs matching vs mask overlay vs instruction rewrite, sensitivity to number/quality/viewpoint diversity of reference images, and comparison to stronger 3D or multi-view grounding approaches.

Real-world evidence is promising but limited: 8 object categories with 20 trials each, closely related generic training tasks for the adapted π0.5 policy, and no statistical uncertainty. This makes the magnitude and robustness of real-world gains harder to judge.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. The paper describes hardware, training, and major models, but does not clearly commit to releasing the new benchmarks, object assets, reference images, real-world data, evaluation scripts, or all prompts/configurations needed to reproduce the reported results.

The hard-prompt baseline uses GPT-4o descriptions with manual correction, which introduces human judgment and possible inconsistency; it is not fully clear how much effort was allowed for baselines versus VAP.

Ethics and safety are underdeveloped. Since the application stores personal-object reference images and deploys robots around user belongings, privacy, consent, data retention, misidentification harms, and safe failure behavior deserve more than the brief future-looking discussion.

strengths: The paper targets a practically important gap in current VLA systems: acting on user-specific object instances rather than only category-level language commands. The problem formulation is clear and relevant for deployed assistive robotics.

The proposed pipeline is simple and well motivated: retrieve the personal object from reference images, segment/track it, visually highlight it, and rewrite the instruction for a frozen VLA. This makes the method easy to understand and potentially useful as a modular add-on.

The evaluation spans multiple settings: two adapted simulation benchmarks, several robot embodiments, multi-view and single-view settings, and a small real-world SO-101 tabletop benchmark. The reported gains over generic VLA, hard textual prompts, and token-learning baselines are large in many cases.

The manuscript includes useful failure analysis, especially distinguishing grounding errors, cross-view inconsistency, and downstream manipulation failures. The limitations discussion is reasonably honest about reliance on detection/segmentation quality, short-horizon tasks, and single personalized objects.
weaknesses: The central contribution is technically modest. VAP is largely a composition of existing modules, DINOv2, Grounding DINO, SAM2, tracking, visual highlighting, and template instruction rewriting. The paper does not provide much new algorithmic insight beyond showing that an off-the-shelf perception stack plus visual prompting helps frozen VLAs.

The evaluation does not sufficiently isolate which component causes the gains. Missing or underdeveloped controls include oracle masks, detector-only/category-box prompts, mask versus box versus tint ablations, instruction-rewrite-only versus visual-only prompting, and comparisons to simpler reference-image retrieval plus explicit action targeting. Without these, it is hard to know whether the claimed VLA personalization mechanism is the right explanation.

The benchmarks appear highly customized and limited in diversity. Several simulation tasks use only a small number of personal categories, and the real-world benchmark has only 8 categories with 20 trials each. The setup is tabletop, short-horizon, and single-target, so the claims about personalized manipulation in daily-life settings feel broader than the evidence supports.

Some baselines are potentially weak or mismatched. The soft-prompt baseline is trained through a proxy VLM recognition task rather than actual VLA control, while the hard-prompt baseline depends on generated textual descriptions. Stronger alternatives such as PerSAM-like personalized segmentation, CLIP/DINO retrieval with direct mask prompting ablations, or learned instance-aware grounding baselines are not convincingly explored.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper lists high-level components, hardware, and some training hyperparameters, but does not specify enough benchmark construction details, asset splits, exact prompts/templates, random seeds, model checkpoints, detector thresholds, tracking parameters, or whether code/assets will be released. Reproducing the custom simulation and real-world results would be difficult.

The reported results lack uncertainty estimates or statistical testing despite small real-world sample sizes and stochastic robot rollouts. This weakens confidence in the magnitude and robustness of the reported improvements.

The method depends heavily on upstream perception quality and cross-view consistency, and the paper itself reports that multi-view failures are often caused by inconsistent prompts. This is a material limitation for real robotic deployment, not just a minor future-work issue.

Ethics and privacy considerations are only briefly gestured at in the discussion. Since the method stores reference images of personal objects and is framed for user-centered robots, the paper should more concretely address consent, data retention, misuse, and failure modes in shared environments.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and well-motivated gap in VLA systems: personalized object manipulation where the robot must identify a user-specific instance among visually similar distractors. The task formulation is useful and practically relevant for household/assistive robotics.

The proposed VAP method is simple, training-free, and technically sensible: reference images are used as a non-parametric memory, open-vocabulary detection plus DINOv2 matching and SAM2 segmentation/tracking produce object masks, and the frozen VLA is guided through pixel-space highlighting plus instruction rewriting. The method is easy to understand and plausibly deployable.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this problem setting. The authors evaluate across Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench, and a real-world SO-101 tabletop setup, covering multiple robots, cameras, object categories, and both selection and pick-and-place tasks.

Results are convincing relative to the baselines. VAP substantially improves correct movement and success rates, e.g. large gains on Personalized-SIMPLER WidowX tasks and real-world pointing/pick-and-place averages. The inclusion of hard-prompt and token-learning baselines makes the comparison more meaningful than testing only against a generic VLA.

The paper provides useful diagnostics beyond aggregate success rates, including CMR, runtime analysis, token-learning attention analysis, and a failure-mode taxonomy separating wrong single-view prompts, multi-view inconsistency, and downstream manipulation failures.

Presentation is generally clear, with helpful figures, tables, benchmark summaries, and appendix details. The limitations discussion is honest and identifies real bottlenecks such as reliance on grounding quality, cross-view inconsistency, short-horizon tabletop scope, and single personalized-object assumptions.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is moderate. VAP is an effective composition of existing perception modules and visual prompting rather than a fundamentally new learning or control method. Its contribution is strongest as a system formulation and empirical demonstration.

The method depends heavily on powerful off-the-shelf components: Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM2, and tracking. The paper does not sufficiently isolate how much of the gain comes from the visual prompt itself versus near-oracle external perception and segmentation. Ablations over detector/encoder/segmenter quality, mask noise, highlight style, and instruction rewriting would strengthen the causal claims.

The benchmarks are valuable but still limited in scope. Most tasks are tabletop, short-horizon, and involve a single personalized object category at a time. It remains unclear how well VAP scales to cluttered homes, multiple personalized objects, changing personal-object appearances, objects without clear category names, or long-horizon tasks requiring repeated re-grounding.

The real-world evaluation is promising but relatively small: 160 trials over 8 object categories in one hardware setup. The reported gains are large, but broader real-world diversity and statistical uncertainty estimates would make the evidence more robust.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The paper gives many implementation details and training settings, but it is not clear whether code, benchmark generation scripts, assets, reference images, trained checkpoints, and real-world data will be released. Some external assets and models may also complicate exact reproduction.

The treatment of privacy and ethics is underdeveloped for a personalization method that stores user-specific object references. The discussion briefly mentions transparency, revocation, and boundaries around personal data, but the main paper lacks a concrete protocol for memory deletion, misuse prevention, consent, or safe behavior when the system misidentifies personal objects.

The soft-prompt baseline is thoughtfully constructed, but it uses a proxy VLM recognition objective rather than end-to-end personalized control data. This is reasonable given the paper's training-free goal, but it leaves open whether stronger learned personalization adapters or retrieval-conditioned policies would narrow the gap.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored robotics problem: manipulating user-specific object instances rather than generic categories. The formulation is practically meaningful and clearly motivated.

The proposed VAP pipeline is simple, modular, and plausible: reference-based candidate matching, segmentation/tracking, mask highlighting, and instruction rewriting are well aligned with the failure mode of frozen VLAs collapsing to category-level semantics.

The empirical evaluation is broader than a typical proof of concept, spanning Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench, and a real SO-101 setup, with same-category distractors and both selection and manipulation tasks.

Results show large and consistent gains over generic VLA, hard-prompt, and token-learning baselines. The real-world improvement from 18.8% to 58.8% average pick-and-place success is especially compelling.
The paper includes useful ablations for instruction rewriting, reference aggregation, number of reference images, and prompt design, plus runtime analysis and a candid failure taxonomy.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate. The main method is a sensible composition of existing open-vocabulary detection, DINOv2 matching, SAM2 segmentation/tracking, visual highlighting, and template rewriting, rather than a fundamentally new learning or control approach.

The evaluation depends heavily on custom benchmark construction and curated personal-object setups. It is hard to judge whether the gains will persist in less controlled household scenes with many categories, severe clutter, changing lighting, or ambiguous natural-language references.

The method assumes that the generic object category can be parsed from a possessive phrase such as 'my cup' and uses deterministic rewriting. This sidesteps more realistic referring expressions, ownership ambiguity, and multi-user language complexity.

The central system is not fully training-free in the broader deployment sense: the VLA is fine-tuned for Personalized-VLABench and real-world environment adaptation, although personal objects are excluded. This is reasonable, but the distinction should be emphasized more carefully.

Multi-view settings expose a serious limitation: over 50% of failures in Personalized-VLABench and real-world experiments are due to cross-view prompt inconsistency. This is acknowledged but left unresolved, limiting the robustness claim.

Real-world evaluation is promising but still small: 8 object categories, 20 trials per task, tabletop-only, and short-horizon tasks. Statistical uncertainty and sensitivity to object choice are not deeply analyzed.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives many implementation details and hyperparameters, but does not clearly commit to releasing code, adapted benchmark assets, trained checkpoints, object references, or real-world data/protocols needed to reproduce the main results.
The paper lacks an explicit ethics or privacy section despite dealing with user-specific personal objects and visual memory. Privacy is only briefly mentioned as future work.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically meaningful gap in current VLA systems: personalized instance-level manipulation among same-category distractors, which is a real limitation of language-only robot instructions.

The proposed VAP pipeline is simple, training-free at deployment, and easy to understand: open-vocabulary detection, reference-image matching, segmentation/tracking, visual mask highlighting, and instruction rewriting.

The evaluation is broader than many robotics papers, covering two simulation benchmarks, multiple robot embodiments, multi-view selection, and a small real-world SO-101 setup. The reported gains over generic VLA, hard-prompt, and soft-token baselines are often large, especially on Personalized-SIMPLER and real-world selection tasks.

The paper includes useful ablations on rewriting, reference aggregation, number of reference images, mask versus box prompting, and highlight opacity. These support the claim that the visual prompt and instruction rewrite must be coupled.

The failure analysis is unusually concrete: the authors separate grounding errors, cross-view inconsistency, and manipulation failures, and they acknowledge that multi-view inconsistency is a major unresolved issue.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is modest. VAP is largely a composition of existing components, Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM2, tracking, visual highlighting, and template rewriting. The paper’s main novelty is packaging and evaluation rather than a new algorithmic idea.

The central claim of personalizing frozen VLAs is somewhat weakened by environment-specific VLA fine-tuning for Personalized-VLABench and the real-world setup. Although personal objects are excluded, the method depends on adapted backbone policies, making it less clear how much generalization comes from VAP versus careful task/environment tuning.

The benchmarks are narrow and partly custom: tabletop scenes, short-horizon tasks, one personalized object at a time, known object category, and same-category distractors. This limits the significance of the conclusion that the approach bridges personalized semantics and control.

The real-world evidence is useful but not fully convincing. It uses only 160 trials over 8 categories, and VAP reaches 58.8% average success on pick-and-place. This is an improvement, but still far from reliable deployment-level personalized manipulation.

The baselines are not fully satisfying. Hard prompts are text-only and soft prompts are trained through a proxy VLM recognition task rather than direct VLA action supervision, so the comparison does not rule out stronger personalized policy adaptation or retrieval-conditioned VLA baselines.

The method relies on brittle assumptions: the system must parse a 'my X' trigger, know the generic category X, detect candidates for that category, and use a fixed color-word rewrite such as 'the red cup'. This is far from natural open-ended personalization.

The multi-view setting exposes a serious unresolved weakness: more than half of VAP failures in multi-view benchmarks are attributed to inconsistent prompts across cameras. Since many real robot systems are multi-view, this is not a minor edge case.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives implementation details and hyperparameters, but the custom benchmarks, Sketchfab asset choices, real-world data, teleoperation data, and code release status are not clearly sufficient for independent replication.

The ethics/privacy treatment is thin. Personalized robots operating over user belongings raise privacy, ownership, consent, and misuse concerns; the paper mentions privacy only briefly in future work rather than treating it as part of the method or evaluation.

Presentation is generally clear, but the paper sometimes overstates the contribution as 'personalizing VLAs' when the system is better described as an external perception-and-prompting pipeline that can fail independently of the VLA.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and practically important problem: VLA policies often handle generic object categories but fail on user-specific instances such as “my cup” among same-category distractors. This is a meaningful formulation for personalized robot assistance.

The proposed Visual Attentive Prompting framework is simple, well motivated, and technically sensible: reference-image retrieval grounds the instance, segmentation/tracking creates a mask, and a matched visual highlight plus instruction rewrite converts personalization into cues that frozen VLAs can exploit.

The empirical evaluation is broad for a robotics paper. The authors construct two simulation benchmarks and a real-world SO-101 tabletop benchmark, covering multiple robots, task types, camera settings, and both selection and pick-and-place tasks.

The results are convincing in aggregate. VAP substantially improves success and correct-movement rates over generic VLA, hard textual prompting, and a strengthened soft-token baseline, with especially large gains on Personalized-SIMPLER and real-world tasks.

The ablations are useful and support the main design choices: mask plus rewrite is far stronger than either alone, segmentation masks beat boxes, reference count matters, and the voting aggregation choice is justified.

The paper is unusually strong in failure analysis. It separates single-view grounding errors, multi-view inconsistency, and downstream control failures, and the appendix gives concrete qualitative examples and plausible future directions.

Presentation is clear and well organized. The figures communicate the task and pipeline effectively, and the appendix contains many implementation details, prompt descriptions, baseline details, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The core method is more of a clever systems composition than a fundamentally new learning algorithm. It relies heavily on existing perception modules such as Grounding DINO, DINOv2, and SAM2, plus a hand-designed visual overlay and template rewrite.

The claim of being training-free needs careful interpretation. VAP itself is per-object training-free, but the paper fine-tunes pi-0.5 for the VLABench and real-world environments using hundreds of generic episodes and substantial compute; this distinction is explained but could be clearer in the main claims.

The real-world benchmark is promising but still limited: 8 tasks, 20 trials per task, tabletop scenes, short horizons, and mostly one personalized target at a time. This leaves open how well the approach scales to homes, deformable objects, occlusions, clutter, moving users, and longer sequential tasks.

The method depends on a fairly specific interface: a parseable possessive phrase such as “my X,” known coarse category, a small curated reference set, and a VLA that responds well to color-highlighted regions and color-word rewrites. More natural language variation is mostly deferred to future parsing extensions.

Multi-view settings reveal a substantial unresolved weakness: over half of the failures in VLABench and real-world settings are attributed to cross-view inconsistency. Since many real robotic systems are multi-camera, this is a material limitation.

The baselines are reasonable, but the evaluation would be stronger with additional upper bounds or competitors, such as oracle masks, stronger instance retrieval/tracking variants, explicit cross-view fusion, or a modular detect-then-act policy that uses the grounded mask without visual prompt rewriting.

Reproducibility is adequate at the level of descriptions and hyperparameters, but the paper does not clearly commit to releasing the new benchmarks, assets, real-world data, code, and evaluation scripts. Reproducing the full real-robot setup and proprietary or future-dated components may be difficult.

Ethical and privacy considerations are only lightly discussed. Since the method stores reference images of personal belongings and is intended for personalized home assistance, the paper should more directly address privacy, consent in shared spaces, misuse risks, and safety failures when the wrong object is manipulated.
